title: China Moves to Lock in a New Edge on Taiwan Before the Next Trump-Xi Summit
author: Di Lu
text:
China Coast Guard vessel 5201 operating near Second Thomas Shoal in the South China Sea, Mar. 21, 2023.
Credit: Philippine Coast Guard
China’s military pressure on Taiwan remained generally stable in the first half of 2026, with no major escalation in military aircraft or naval vessel activity. Tensions ran lower than at the end of 2025. This owes largely to the multiple opportunities for direct meetings that the U.S. and Chinese leaders arranged in 2026. For example, during the mid-May 2026 summit between Xi Jinping and Donald Trump, from May 13 to 17, daily sorties by Chinese military aircraft detected around Taiwan fell to an average of three, with zero sorties on both May 14 and May 15. By comparison, the daily average for the first half of 2026 was 7.5 sorties. After the summit concluded, the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) conducted a joint combat readiness patrol on May 19; Taiwan’s Ministry of National Defense detected 24 military aircraft that day.[...]
